concerns.text: The baseline is computed from a single noise‑free trajectory per system dimension (N). This provides no estimate of baseline variability, yet Δλ is defined as the difference from this single value. If the baseline itself fluctuates across runs, the deviation metric will inherit that noise, potentially biasing regression results. A more robust approach would compute multiple baselines per N (e.g., several long clean trajectories) and propagate their variance into Δλ.

The mixed‑effects model includes a random intercept per trajectory but treats each sliding‑window FTLE estimate as an independent observation. Overlapping windows from the same trajectory are highly correlated, violating the independence assumption and inflating effective sample size. Consider adding random slopes for window size or explicitly modeling the within‑trajectory autocorrelation structure.

The power analysis assumes 1 080 independent observations, yet the dependence described above (overlapping windows, shared baselines) reduces the effective sample size. Consequently, the claimed ≥ 80 % power to detect a small‑to‑medium effect may be optimistic. Re‑estimate power using the actual hierarchical design (e.g., simulation with the proposed random‑effects structure).
Phase 0 (Bootstrap) is listed without any FR or SC reference. The spec does not require a bootstrap step, so this task is not traceable to a functional requirement or success criterion.
Phase 7 (Artifact Bundling & Validation) performs bundling and checksum recording but does not cite any FR or SC. While useful for hygiene, it is not linked to a concrete requirement in the spec.
Phase 9 (CI / Testing) asserts verification of “All FRs” but does not map to any specific SC (e.g., SC‑004 runtime limit). The effort is not explicitly tied to a success criterion.
Phase 10 (Documentation) updates README and quickstart but has no associated FR or SC in the specification.

The mixed‑effects regression treats each sliding‑window FTLE estimate as an independent observation with only a random intercept per trajectory. Because windows overlap within a single trajectory, their errors are serially correlated beyond what a random intercept captures. Applying a Durbin‑Watson test on the FTLE time‑series and then using Newey‑West HAC correction on the regression residuals does not fully address the hierarchical autocorrelation structure. A more appropriate model would include a random slope for window size or explicitly model the within‑trajectory correlation (e.g., using a covariance structure for repeated measures).

The baseline for each window size is computed with Rosenstein’s algorithm on the clean trajectory, while noisy FTLEs are computed with a QR‑based method. Although the algorithms differ, the baseline values are deterministic functions of the same underlying system and are used as fixed offsets (Δλ). This makes the dependent variable (Δλ) partially a deterministic transformation of the predictor ‘window size’ (T) rather than a purely stochastic outcome, which can inflate apparent significance of the 1/T term. The analysis should treat the baseline uncertainty (e.g., via its convergence error) as part of the error model rather than assuming it is exact.
